newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU Commission weighs four or six new EU members.
newsitem.headline: EU Commission weighs four or six new EU members.

text.p: The European Commission was locked in intensive discussions on Thursday to decide how many and which countries should be invited to the first eastwards expansion of the European Union.
The crucial all-day session, forecast to last well into the evening, could determine whether Slovenia and Estonia join Poland, the Czech Republic, Hungary and Cyprus in a first wave of entry talks.

The 20 Commissioners went to the talks divided into two camps over whether the 15-nation bloc's first foray behind the former Iron Curtain should embrace just the three eastern frontrunners or the Baltic state of Estonia and the former Yugoslav state of Slovenia as well.

Faced with bitter disappointment on the part of five other applicants -- Latvia, Lithuania, Slovakia, Romania and Bulgaria -- judged not yet ready, but still deperate to join, Commissioners were also discussing what kind of waiting room to set up to keep them involved.

The EU's External Relations Commissioner Hans van den Broek presented the 20 commissioners with detailed assessments of how suitable 10 eastern countries are for the economic and political rigours of EU membership.

Although Van den Broek has strong backing for his plan to extend to five eastern countries in the first instance, powerful forces in the Commission surrounding Commission President Jacques Santer went to the meeting demanding a smaller expansion to avoid an EU institutional overhaul.

The Commission will take a final decision on which countries to recommend to EU governments -- who have final say -- next Tuesday in Strasbourg, but EU officials did not exclude the issue being settled at Thursday's meeting.

The plan to take in five new countries has a long list of supporters, including British Commissioners Sir Leon Brittan and Neil Kinnock, German Commissioner Martin Bangemann, Sweden's Commissioner Anita Gradin, Denmark's Ritt Bjerregaard and southern Commissioners such as Greece's Christos Papoutis.

Several officials predicted that, with Santer gradually coming round to the merits of the two countries, the Commission would finally come down in favour of opening talks with five eastern countries, plus Cyprus, after a struggle.

The backers say that if the EU is to honour its commitment to judge the applications by the eastern countries on objective criteria, Estonia and Slovenia should be admitted on the same basis as Poland

But Commissioners from smaller countries, led by Santer, fear that by taking in five eastern countries the EU will commit itself to lengthy and difficult institutional reforms which could delay the enlargement and sap the power of the EU's smaller countries.

At the heart of the problem is the failure of EU leaders to agree at their June 16-17 Amsterdam summit on the institutional reforms necessary to loosen up the bloc's decision-making procedures for the day it has up to a dozen new members.
Under the fudge agreed at Amsterdam the EU must hold a new treaty-revising conference if it expands to more than 20 members.
As Cyprus has already been in line for some time and is heavily backed by Greece, the number of EU members would expand to 21 if it was admitted along with five easterners.
